## Hilar Cholangiocarcinoma: Standard and Extended Resections

- Chapter 119B
- Volume 2
- Topic: standard and extended resections of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma

## Scope of This Presentation

- Overview of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma
- Preoperative radiologic evaluation
- Standard resection
- Extended resection
- Combined vascular resection
- Hepatopancreatoduodenectomy
- Tables and figures from the chapter
- Technical principles and anatomic pitfalls

## Why Perihilar Cholangiocarcinoma Is Devastating

- Most patients present with advanced disease
- Initial diagnosis is often late
- Cure is uncommon without complete surgical removal
- The hilum contains critical vessels and bile ducts in a compact space
- Small errors in anatomic recognition can cause major complications

## Surgical Cure and Margin Goal

- Surgical resection is the only current possibility of cure
- Achieving tumor-free surgical margins is a primary goal
- Positive margins lead to unsatisfactory long-term outcomes
- Margin status depends on precise hilar dissection
- Preoperative planning and intraoperative anatomy knowledge are essential

## Evolution From Local Bile Duct Resection

- Earlier operations often used hilar bile duct resection alone
- Limited hepatectomy was sometimes added
- These approaches frequently resulted in positive margins
- Long-term outcomes were unsatisfactory
- Modern surgery has shifted toward formal hepatic resection

## Current Standard Operation

- Hemihepatectomy with bile duct resection is now standard
- Caudate lobectomy is routinely included
- Regional lymph node dissection is performed
- Bilioenteric continuity is restored after resection
- The procedure is designed to improve margin clearance

## Extended Resections for Advanced Disease

- Some centers perform more extensive operations for selected patients
- Extended procedures include:
  - Hepatic trisectionectomy
  - Combined resection with reconstruction of hepatic inflow vessels
  - Hepatectomy combined with pancreatoduodenectomy
- These operations aim to increase resectability
- They are technically demanding and not universal

## Why Technical Expertise Is Limited

- Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma is rare
- Tumor anatomy and vascular anatomy vary widely
- Many surgeons see limited cases
- Accumulation of expertise is difficult
- Technical detail matters because small anatomic variations can create major operative difficulty

## Purpose of This Presentation

- Describe technical details of standard resections
- Describe technical details of extended resections
- Highlight anatomic variations associated with difficulty
- Cover figures and tables in a slide-based format
- Emphasize practical operative sequence and pitfalls

## Preoperative Radiologic Evaluation

- Precise anatomic knowledge is crucial for surgical success
- The surgeon must understand:
  - Segmental liver anatomy
  - Hepatic inflow vessels
  - Hepatic outflow vessels
  - Biliary channel anatomy
- Imaging helps avoid inadvertent injury to preserved structures

## Need for Precise Segmental Anatomy

- The hilar vasculature differs from case to case
- The relationship among hepatic arteries, portal veins, and bile ducts must be evaluated
- Segmental anatomy guides the planned resection
- Misidentification can compromise the remnant liver
- Preoperative mapping supports safe vascular division

## Multidetector CT and 3D Reconstruction

- Dynamic enhanced multidetector-row CT is used
- Multiplanar three-dimensional images are reconstructed
- These images help identify:
  - Ramification pattern of hepatic arteries
  - Running course of hepatic arteries
  - Portal vein anatomy
- They also help evaluate vascular involvement

## CT Before Biliary Drainage

- When CT is obtained before biliary drainage, dilated bile ducts are visible
- The anatomic relationship between vessels and dilated biliary trees can be identified
- This can improve understanding of hilar distortion
- Timing of imaging should be considered in obstructive jaundice
- The goal is better preoperative anatomic definition

## Individual Hilar Vascular Anatomy

- Hilar vascular anatomy is highly variable
- Arteries, portal veins, and bile ducts must be evaluated together
- Vascular involvement must be assessed before surgery
- Three-dimensional imaging supports operative planning
- Individual anatomy determines the safe dissection pathway

## Standard Resection: Components

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Right or left hemihepatectomy | Removes involved liver territory |
| Caudate lobectomy | Clears frequent caudate invasion |
| Bile duct resection | Removes extrahepatic biliary tumor burden |
| Lymph node dissection | Improves staging and local clearance |
| Bilioenteric anastomosis | Restores biliary drainage |

## Tumor Origin Around the Hilum

- Perihilar tumors may originate from:
  - Right hepatic duct
  - Left hepatic duct
  - Biliary confluence
  - Upper bile duct
  - Hepatic parenchyma adjacent to the hilum
- Origin influences local spread
- Tumors frequently invade nearby portal structures and bile ducts

## Caudate Lobe Involvement

- Tumors frequently invade portal structures and bile ducts of the caudate lobe
- Preoperative imaging often underestimates caudate infiltration
- Caudate lobectomy is required for curative resection
- Omitting caudate resection risks residual disease
- The caudate lobe is therefore removed with the hemiliver

## Indications for Standard Resection

- Standard resections are indicated for Bismuth type I tumors
- They are also indicated for Bismuth type II tumors
- They are used for Bismuth type III tumors
- Macrovascular invasion should be absent for standard resection as described here
- The goal remains complete tumor removal with negative margins

## Standard Resection Sequence

| Step | Operative Action |
|---|---|
| Step 1 | Lymphadenectomy with division of the distal bile duct |
| Step 2 | Vascular division of the hemiliver in the hepatic hilum |
| Step 3 | Mobilization of the hemiliver and caudate lobe |
| Step 4 | Liver parenchymal transection |
| Step 5 | Division of the proximal intrahepatic bile duct |

## Operative Incision Choices

- Several incisions can be used for laparotomy
- The authors preferentially use an upper midline incision
- The incision extends cephalad to the xiphoid process
- A right transverse incision may reach the anterior axillary line
- This creates a reverse L incision
- In some overweight patients, the transverse incision is extended to the left anterior axillary line as a reverse T incision

## Initial Exploration and Kocher Maneuver

- The abdomen is inspected for distant metastasis
- Peritoneal dissemination is assessed
- The curve of the duodenum is mobilized by the Kocher maneuver
- Periaortic lymph nodes are evaluated for staging
- This early assessment helps determine resectability

## Lymphadenectomy: Main Goal

- Achieve a negative margin at the distal bile duct
- Perform thorough regional lymph node dissection
- Remove nodes in key stations around the hilum and pancreas
- Provide accurate pathologic staging
- Improve local disease clearance

## Regional Lymph Node Stations

| Station Group | Anatomic Area |
|---|---|
| Hilar nodes | Hepatic hilum |
| Cystic nodes | Near gallbladder and cystic duct |
| Choledochal nodes | Along bile duct |
| Portal nodes | Around portal vein |
| Hepatic arterial nodes | Along hepatic arteries |
| Posterior pancreaticoduodenal nodes | Behind pancreas and duodenum |

## Lymph Node Count and Survival

- A sufficient number of lymph nodes must be retrieved
- Accurate staging depends on node examination
- Recent studies show that the number of lymph nodes examined is associated with survival
- This association is particularly important in node-negative patients
- Adequate lymphadenectomy is therefore not optional

## Starting Lymphadenectomy in the Lesser Sac

- The authors prefer to begin by opening the lesser sac
- This displays lymph nodes cranioventral to the common hepatic artery
- The approach improves exposure
- It helps define arterial anatomy early
- It creates a controlled plane for node dissection

## Exposing the Common Hepatic Artery

- Lymph nodes are detached from the pancreas
- The nodes are flipped up cranially
- This exposes the common hepatic artery
- The bifurcation into the gastroduodenal artery and proper hepatic artery is identified
- Vascular control supports safe lymphadenectomy

## Gastropancreatic Fold and Left Gastric Artery

- Retraction of the gastropancreatic fold to the left improves the surgical view
- This facilitates lymph node dissection
- It also helps avoid inadvertent injury to the left gastric artery
- Controlled retraction is important in this step
- The arterial anatomy becomes clearer

## Dividing the Common Bile Duct

- The visceral peritoneum on the hepatoduodenal ligament is cut
- The cut begins at the superior aspect of the duodenum
- The duodenal bulb is pulled down
- The common bile duct is isolated
- The duct is cut at the entry of the pancreatic head as far from the tumor edge as possible

## Distal Margin Frozen Section

- The common bile duct stump is closed with sutures
- The distal bile duct margin is submitted for frozen section examination
- The goal is a satisfactory ductal margin length
- Frozen section guides whether additional resection is needed
- Margin assessment is central to curative intent

## Additional Intrapancreatic Bile Duct Resection

- If the distal margin is positive on frozen section, additional resection is possible
- The intrapancreatic bile duct can be resected further
- This can increase margin length
- The technique helps avoid leaving distal ductal disease
- It is an important rescue maneuver during standard resection

## Identifying and Taping the Portal Vein

- The portal vein is identified posteriorly
- It is taped between the dissected common bile duct and the proper hepatic artery
- The proper hepatic artery is taped beforehand
- This relationship helps define the hepatoduodenal ligament anatomy
- Safe vascular identification precedes further dissection

## Posterior Pancreaticoduodenal Lymph Nodes

- Posterior pancreaticoduodenal lymph nodes are detached
- Dissection proceeds from the posterior surface of the duodenum and pancreas head
- Tiny vessels leading to lymph nodes are cautiously ligated and cut
- Meticulous hemostasis is required
- The nodes are removed in continuity with the specimen when appropriate

## Completing Pancreatoduodenal Node Dissection

- Lymph nodes dorsal to the portal vein and common hepatic artery are dissected
- These nodes are removed in conjunction with posterior pancreaticoduodenal nodes
- Dissection around the pancreatoduodenum is completed
- Dissection around the common hepatic artery is completed
- This completes the lower field lymphadenectomy

## Opening the Hepatoduodenal Ligament

- The peritoneum of the hepatoduodenal ligament is opened upward to the hepatic hilum
- Lymph nodes in the ligament are completely dissected
- The covering peritoneum is cut just in front of the proper hepatic artery
- This facilitates isolation of the artery and its bifurcation
- Connective tissue in front of the portal vein is divided to expose the main portal vein

## Isolating Proper Hepatic Artery and Portal Vein

- The proper hepatic artery is isolated
- Its bifurcation into right and left hepatic arteries is identified
- The main portal vein is successively exposed
- The hilar dissection becomes more defined
- This prepares the field for vascular division

## Right Hepatectomy: Vascular Division Overview

- The left hepatic artery supplying segments II and III is isolated
- The middle hepatic artery supplying segment IV is isolated
- The left portal vein is isolated
- These structures are detached from the hilar plate
- The right hepatic artery and right portal vein are ligated and cut at the origin

## Preserving Left and Middle Hepatic Arteries

- The left and middle hepatic arteries are isolated upward to the base of the umbilical fossa
- This is done after dividing the right hepatic artery
- The left hepatic artery commonly runs into the umbilical fossa
- It lies to the left of the elbow of the left portal vein
- It runs in front of the ligamentum venosum

## Middle Hepatic Artery Anatomy

- The middle hepatic artery supplies segment IV
- It normally originates from the proper, right, or left hepatic artery
- It traverses the left portal vein into the umbilical fossa
- It lies to the right of the elbow of the left portal vein
- Recognition prevents inadvertent injury during right-sided resection

## Caudate Arterial Branches

- Small arterial branches to the caudate lobe may arise from the left hepatic artery
- They may also arise from the middle hepatic artery at the hepatic hilus
- These branches must be cautiously ligated and divided
- Failure to control them can cause bleeding or incomplete caudate resection
- Careful hilar dissection is required

## Right Portal Vein Division

- The right portal vein is cut at the bifurcation
- The division occurs after left portal vein identification
- Small portal branches to the caudate lobe are addressed separately
- The left portal vein must be protected
- Precise division supports complete removal of the right hemiliver

## Caudate Portal Branches From Left Portal Vein

- Several small portal branches to the caudate lobe originate from the transverse portion of the left portal vein
- These branches are ligated and cut cautiously
- The transverse portion of the left portal vein is then detached from the hilar plate
- This step clears the caudate inflow
- It also improves exposure for proximal bile duct division

## Detaching the Hilar Plate in Right Hepatectomy

- The ligamentum venosum is dissected left posteriorly to the elbow of the left portal vein
- The transverse portion of the left portal vein is fully detached from the hilar plate
- Division of the hilar portal vein is then completed
- This mobilization is essential for safe ductal transection
- It defines the future bile duct cut line

## Importance of Hilar Detachment for Duct Margin

- The future cut line of the left hepatic bile duct lies near the umbilical portion of the left portal vein
- It is just to the right on the cranial side of the umbilical portion
- It is next to the hepatic entry of the middle hepatic artery
- The resection line of the proximal bile duct depends on the extent of hilar dissection
- Sufficient detachment is mandatory

## Left Hepatectomy: Vascular Division Overview

- The right hepatic artery and right portal vein are isolated
- They are detached from the hilar plate
- The middle and left hepatic arteries are ligated and cut at the origin
- The left portal vein is ligated and cut at the origin
- The right-sided inflow structures are preserved

## Right Hepatic Artery Involvement

- The right hepatic artery normally runs just behind the hilar tumor
- It is susceptible to involvement
- If involvement is confirmed during surgery, combined resection of the hepatic artery is considered
- Reconstructability must be assessed
- This decision is critical in left-sided resections

## Right Anterior and Posterior Hepatic Arteries

- After division of the left and middle hepatic arteries and cystic artery, the right hepatic artery is detached from the posterior wall of the hilar bile duct
- The dissected common bile duct is flipped up and retracted cranioventrally
- The artery is isolated distally toward its bifurcation
- The right anterior hepatic artery normally runs into the hepatic entry between the right anterior portal vein and right hepatic bile duct
- The right posterior hepatic artery runs into the hepatic entry at Rouviere's sulcus, farther from the hilar bile ducts

## Supraportal Right Posterior Hepatic Artery

- In a minority of cases, the right posterior hepatic artery or its branch separates from the right hepatic artery
- It may run along the left side of the right anterior hepatic artery
- It may run cranially to the right portal vein
- This is called the supraportal type or combined type
- The artery then lies close to the right hilar ducts and right anterior hepatic artery, requiring cautious isolation

## Portal Vein Division in Left Hepatectomy

- The left portal vein is cut at the portal bifurcation
- Small portal branches to the caudate lobe originating from the right portal trunk are ligated and cut cautiously
- The right portal trunk is isolated from the hilar plate toward the hepatic entry
- Division of hilar vascular structures is then completed
- Preservation of right-sided portal inflow is essential

## Detachment for Right Hilar Duct Margin

- The right anterior hepatic artery and right portal vein or right anterior portal vein must be detached from the ductal system as proximally as possible
- The future hepatic bile duct margin lies just cranial to these structures
- The resection line depends on the extent of hilar dissection
- Incomplete detachment risks a positive proximal margin
- This step is central to left hepatectomy for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma

## Mobilization of Hemiliver and Caudate Lobe

- Liver mobilization is similar to formal right or left hepatectomy
- The hemiliver is mobilized together with the caudate lobe
- The authors prefer mobilization from the same side as the resection
- Right-sided hepatectomy uses right-sided mobilization
- Left-sided hepatectomy uses left-sided mobilization

## Preserving Collateral Arterial Supply

- Collateral artery branches from the phrenic artery may supply the remnant liver
- Collateral branches from the adrenal artery may also be important
- These branches are preserved as much as possible
- Preservation supports remnant liver perfusion
- This is especially important after major hepatectomy

## Short Hepatic Veins and Inferior Vena Cava

- The caudate lobe is detached from the anterior surface of the inferior vena cava
- Many short hepatic veins are encountered
- These veins are ligated and divided
- Careful handling prevents major venous bleeding
- The inferior vena cava is progressively exposed

## IVC Ligament and Ligamentum Venosum

- On the upper side of the inferior vena cava, the IVC ligament is dissected
- This thin band-like connective tissue bridges both edges of the caval groove
- The ligamentum venosum connects to the confluence of the middle and left hepatic veins
- It is cut at the distal end
- This completes upper caudate mobilization

## Right-Sided Mobilization Details

- In right-sided hepatectomy, dissection of the right hepatic vein facilitates exposure
- It improves the surgical view for mobilization of the caudate lobe
- The right hemiliver and caudate lobe are mobilized together
- The inferior vena cava is exposed as needed
- This approach supports safe parenchymal transection

## Left-Sided Mobilization Details

- In left-sided hepatectomy, the caudate lobe is fully detached from the anterior part of the inferior vena cava
- The right border of the inferior vena cava is exposed
- The common trunk of the middle and left hepatic veins is taped
- This helps control hepatic venous outflow
- It also clarifies the upper transection plane

## Liver Parenchymal Transection: Demarcation

- The hepatic artery and portal vein to the resected hemiliver are controlled
- The right and left liver become demarcated on the surface
- Discoloration of the hemiliver to be resected appears
- The surface demarcation guides transection
- This visual cue is used to set the parenchymal cut line

## Transection Line on Liver Surfaces

| Surface | Right Hepatectomy | Left Hepatectomy |
|---|---|---|
| Upper surface | Along demarcation line projected from medial margin of gallbladder bed to left of inferior vena cava | Same principle, aligned with demarcation |
| Undersurface | Along medial margin of gallbladder bed to the right of the base of the umbilical fossa | Along craniomedial margin to the hepatic entry of the right anterior hepatic duct |

## Transection Instruments and Inflow Clamping

- The authors prefer a cavitron ultrasonic surgical aspirator
- An instrument facilitating the fracture technique may also be used
- Intermittent hepatic inflow vessel clamping is applied
- Clamping may last 15 or 20 minutes
- Five-minute intervals are used between clamping periods

## Middle Hepatic Vein Preservation

- Parenchymal transection begins along the demarcation line
- The middle hepatic vein is exposed and preserved
- Preservation continues toward the hepatic venous confluence
- Transection proceeds until it reaches the confluence of the middle hepatic vein
- This helps maintain venous drainage of the remnant liver

## Turning the Transection Plane

- In right hepatectomy, the transection direction turns left just ventrally to the ligamentum venosum
- In left hepatectomy, the direction turns posteriorly toward the right edge of the inferior vena cava
- The plane must follow the intended resection boundary
- Careful orientation prevents injury to preserved structures
- The caudate lobe is included in the specimen

## Dividing the Proximal Bile Duct

- In right hepatectomy, intrahepatic bile ducts are isolated and dissected to the right side of the umbilical portion of the left portal vein
- In left hepatectomy, ducts are divided cranially to the right portal vein or right anterior portal vein
- The proximal duct margin is then divided
- The cut line depends on prior hilar dissection
- Frozen section assessment may guide further ductal resection

## Reconstruction After Resection

- After specimen removal, several bile duct orifices may be identified at the proximal stump
- These orifices may be separate and distant from each other
- If possible, they are sutured for unification
- The goal is a secure bilioenteric anastomosis
- Reconstruction restores bile flow to the intestine

## Roux-en-Y Hepaticojejunostomy

- Bilioenteric continuity is re-established by Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
- The jejunal limb is cut approximately 20 to 30 cm on the anal side from the Treitz ligament
- The limb is brought through the mesocolon
- It traverses the lesser sac between pancreas and stomach
- This route reaches the hepatic hilum

## Retrocolic-Retrogastric Jejunal Route

- The retrocolic-retrogastric route is preferentially used
- The jejunal limb easily reaches the intrahepatic bile duct stump
- This route works irrespective of the thickness of the transverse mesocolon
- It also works irrespective of the greater omentum
- It provides a reliable path to the hilum

## Bilioenteric Anastomosis Technique

- Anastomosis is performed with mucosa-to-mucosa alignment
- Continuous or interrupted sutures may be used
- Five-zero absorbable monofilament sutures are preferred
- Precise mucosal approximation is important
- The aim is a patent, leak-resistant bilioenteric connection

## External Biliary Stents

- External stents may be inserted through the stump of the jejunal limb
- They are not always necessary
- The authors prefer to employ them
- They facilitate anastomosis
- They help with postoperative biliary decompression and may prevent severe obstructive cholangitis

## Extended Resection: Hepatic Trisectionectomy

- Hepatic trisectionectomy is used for more advanced tumors
- It may be right-sided or left-sided
- It removes more liver than standard hemihepatectomy
- It can increase the chance of negative proximal margins
- It requires special technical expertise

## Bismuth Type IV Tumors and Resectability

| Historical View | Modern View |
|---|---|
| Bismuth type IV tumors were considered unresectable | Many type IV tumors can be resected |
| Standard hepatectomy often failed to achieve negative margins | Trisectionectomy can achieve negative margins |
| The old concept was followed for a long time | The concept is no longer valid in experienced centers |

## Right Trisectionectomy: Vascular Division

- Lymphadenectomy and liver mobilization are similar to right hepatectomy
- The right hepatic artery and right portal vein are divided
- Hepatic artery and portal branches supplying segment IV are also divided
- This extends the resection beyond classic right hepatectomy
- The left lateral sector is preserved

## Middle Hepatic Artery in Right Trisectionectomy

- The hepatic artery supplying segment IV is known as the middle hepatic artery
- It normally originates extrahepatically from the left, right, or proper hepatic artery
- It is divided at the origin
- This removes segment IV inflow
- The left hepatic artery to segments II and III is preserved

## Anomalous Common Trunk to Segments II, III, and IV

- In a minority of cases, a common trunk supplies segments II, III, and IV
- This trunk may enter to the left or right of the base of the umbilical portion of the left portal vein
- It ramifies into segment IV artery and arteries to segments II and III cranially to the umbilical portion
- The segment IV artery is ligated and divided by opening the umbilical fossa
- The artery to segments II and III must be cautiously detached from the hilar plate behind the umbilical portion

## Portal Branches to Segment IV

- The umbilical portion of the left portal vein is exposed
- The serosa on the right side of the umbilical fossa is dissected
- Portal branches supplying segment IV are isolated at the origin
- This follows division of the right portal vein and detachment of the transverse portion of the left portal vein
- Small portal branches from the cranial side of the umbilical portion are carefully ligated and divided

## Mobilizing the Umbilical Portion

- The umbilical portion of the left portal vein is rotated to the left
- The proximal side of the ligamentum venosum is ligated and divided cranially to the elbow of the left portal vein
- The cranial side of the umbilical portion is completely detached from the umbilical plate
- This allows more proximal left hepatic duct resection
- It is a key technical step in right trisectionectomy

## Right Trisectionectomy: Parenchymal Transection

- The left medial and lateral sectors are demarcated by discoloration of the left medial sector
- The upper transection line aligns with the demarcation line
- It projects through a plane from the round ligament anteriorly to the left of the inferior vena cava posteriorly
- Parenchyma is transected on the left side of the falciform ligament
- The root of the middle hepatic vein is dissected at the confluence of the left hepatic vein

## Dividing Left Lateral Bile Ducts

- The umbilical portion of the left portal vein is retracted to the left
- Bile ducts of the left lateral sector are divided on the left side of the umbilical portion
- Division occurs proximal to the confluence of bile ducts from segments II and III
- Before duct division, the bile ducts are rechecked
- They must be sufficiently detached from left lateral sectional branches of the left portal vein and left hepatic artery

## Margin Benefit of Right Trisectionectomy

| Procedure | Negative Proximal Duct Margin in Selected Bismuth Type IV Tumors |
|---|---|
| Right hepatectomy | 57 percent |
| Anatomic right trisectionectomy | 89 percent |

- Right trisectionectomy allows resection approximately 10 mm beyond the confluence compared with classic right hepatectomy
- This improves proximal duct clearance in right-sided predominance

## Left Trisectionectomy: Vascular Division

- Lymphadenectomy and mobilization are similar to left hepatectomy
- The left and middle hepatic arteries and left portal vein are divided
- The hepatic artery and portal vein supplying the right anterior sector are also dissected
- The right posterior portal vein is detached from the hepatic hilus
- Portal branches to the caudate lobe are divided first

## Right Posterior Hepatic Artery Anomaly in Left Trisectionectomy

- The right posterior hepatic artery normally bifurcates from the right hepatic artery
- It normally runs caudally to the right portal vein and enters the liver at Rouviere's sulcus
- In a minority of cases, it or its branch runs cranially to the right portal vein
- This is the supraportal or combined type
- In such cases, the artery may run to the left of the right anterior hepatic artery near the origin and enter between the right portal vein and hilar bile ducts

## Left Trisectionectomy: Parenchymal Challenges

- Left trisectionectomy is uncommon
- It accounts for less than 5 percent of procedures in several large series
- The right intersectional plate is not always flat
- The right anterior sector may overhang cranially to the right posterior sector
- Clear landmarks on the transection surface may be absent because the right hepatic vein does not always emerge on the transection surface

## Preserving the Right Hepatic Vein

- Parenchymal division can become time-consuming
- Blood loss may increase
- The transection might follow the wrong direction dorsally to the cranial part of the right hepatic vein
- The hepatic parenchyma is therefore cautiously transected
- The right hepatic vein is preserved as the only drainage vein from the liver remnant

## Dividing the Right Posterior Bile Duct

- After liver transection, the right posterior bile duct is divided
- Division occurs at the craniodorsal side of the right posterior portal vein
- In a minority of cases, the right posterior bile duct or its branch runs ventrally and caudally to the right portal vein
- In those cases, it can be divided before liver resection
- This approach allows more proximal bile duct resection

## Margin Benefit of Left Trisectionectomy

| Procedure | Negative Proximal Duct Margin in Selected Bismuth Type IV Tumors |
|---|---|
| Left hepatectomy | 84 percent |
| Left trisectionectomy | 97 percent |

- Left trisectionectomy can resect the right posterior bile duct approximately 7 mm beyond the confluence compared with classic left hepatectomy
- This increases negative proximal margins in left-sided predominance by 13 percent

## Combined Vascular Resection Overview

- Advanced perihilar cholangiocarcinomas often involve contiguous hepatic inflow vascular structures
- This involvement occurs because of anatomic closeness
- Negative surgical margins may be precluded by vascular involvement
- Combined hepatectomy with vascular reconstruction can remove such tumors
- It provides a chance for complete tumor eradication with negative margins

## Three Modes of Combined Vascular Resection

| Mode | Structures Resected |
|---|---|
| Portal vein resection alone | Portal vein segment or wall |
| Hepatic artery resection alone | Involved hepatic artery |
| Simultaneous resection | Portal vein and hepatic artery |

- Each mode requires detailed preoperative vascular evaluation
- Delicate operative technique is mandatory

## Portal Vein Resection: Practical Points

- Portal vein resection is combined with hepatectomy and trisectionectomy
- The portal bifurcation, including right and left portal trunk, is vulnerable to tumor involvement
- This combined method is widely performed in major centers
- Clinical benefit has been validated in many studies
- Segmental portal vein resection is usually easier with right-sided hepatectomy than with left-sided hepatectomy

## Evaluating Portal Vein Reconstructability

- Portal vein involvement may be suspected preoperatively or intraoperatively
- Resectability and reconstructability must be evaluated early
- Isolating the portal vein distal to the involvement is one key to success
- This determines reconstructability
- Safe margins for reconstruction must be obtained

## Distal Portal Vein Isolation by Procedure

| Procedure | Distal Isolation Target |
|---|---|
| Right-sided hepatectomy | Distal end of transverse portion of left portal vein |
| Left hepatectomy | Right portal vein just proximal to bifurcation into right anterior and posterior portal vein |
| Left trisectionectomy | Right posterior portal vein at Rouviere's sulcus |

- Caudate portal branches are carefully ligated and divided during isolation

## Timing of Portal Vein Reconstruction

- Resection and reconstruction of the portal vein are preferentially performed at the final step
- This occurs immediately after removing the specimen
- The surgical view becomes optimal for vascular clamp placement
- Suturing is easier with better exposure
- Final-step reconstruction supports precision

## Segmental Portal Vein Resection and Anastomosis

- Segmental resection followed by direct end-to-end anastomosis is used in most cases
- Posterior wall repair uses a continuous intraluminal suture
- Anterior wall repair uses an extraluminal over-and-over suture
- Five-zero or six-zero nonabsorbable sutures are used
- Tension-free reconstruction is essential

## Wedge Resection and Patch Repair

- Wedge resection followed by direct suture closure is possible
- Patch graft repair is another alternative
- These options are used when the involved area is sufficiently small
- The goal is to preserve portal flow
- Reconstruction should avoid stenosis or tension

## Autogenous Vein Grafts for Portal Vein

- If direct end-to-end anastomosis is not possible, an autogenous vein graft is recommended
- It reduces tension of the reconstructed portal vein
- It helps avoid bleeding from the anastomosis
- It helps avoid portal vein thrombosis
- It helps avoid stenosis after reconstruction

## External Iliac Vein Graft Harvest

- Possible autogenous vein graft sources include:
  - Left renal vein
  - External jugular vein
  - External iliac vein
- The authors prefer a right external iliac vein graft
- It has a similar diameter to the portal vein
- A greater length can be harvested compared with other autogenous vessels
- Harvest uses an extraperitoneal approach through another lower pararectal incision

## Hepatic Artery Resection: Controversy and Outcomes

- Adoption of combined hepatic artery resection for biliary cancers has been controversial
- Previous studies reported conflicting results
- The authors reported a relatively lower mortality rate of 4 percent
- They also reported 5-year overall survival of 27 percent in a large number of patients
- Careful selection and technique are essential

## Arterial Involvement by Tumor Side

- The left hepatic artery runs along the leftmost portion of the hepatoduodenal ligament
- The right hepatic artery crosses the upper bile duct
- Right-sided perihilar tumors rarely involve the left hepatic artery
- Left-sided tumors occasionally involve the right hepatic artery
- Major hepatectomies with hepatic artery resection and reconstruction are therefore predominantly applied in left-sided hepatectomies

## Evaluating Hepatic Artery Reconstructability

- Hepatic artery involvement may be suspected preoperatively or during surgery
- Resectability and reconstructability must be evaluated early
- Isolation of the right hepatic artery during left hepatectomy is key
- Isolation of the right posterior hepatic artery during left trisectionectomy distal to involvement is also key
- This mostly determines reconstructability

## Isolating the Right Posterior Hepatic Artery

- The right posterior hepatic artery normally runs caudally to the right portal vein
- It is distant from the hilar tumor at the hepatic entry
- The artery can be safely isolated
- The covering peritoneum is cut in front of Rouviere's sulcus
- In anomalous cases, isolation posterior to the right posterior portal vein is highly technically demanding

## Timing of Hepatic Artery Resection

- Hepatic artery resection is performed at the final step of hepatic parenchymal transection
- It occurs after dissecting the proximal bile ducts
- It is performed immediately before removing the specimen
- If hepatic arteries perfusing the future resected liver have not been divided because of involvement, hepatic venous outflows are preserved until arterial division
- This avoids excessive congestion of the specimen

## Alternative Timing for Arterial Reconstruction

- In some conditions, resection and reconstruction of the hepatic artery before hepatic parenchymal transection is an alternative
- This may be chosen when feasible
- It can help manage inflow control
- It may reduce congestion issues
- The choice depends on intraoperative circumstances

## Microscopic Hepatic Artery Reconstruction

- The hepatic artery is reconstructed under a microscope
- Nine-zero or ten-zero monofilament nonabsorbable sutures are used
- End-to-end anastomosis is possible in most cases
- Microsurgical technique improves precision
- Patency of the reconstructed artery is critical

## Arterial Graft Options

- Direct end-to-end anastomosis is preferred when possible
- If not possible, the distal cut end may be anastomosed with other visceral arteries
- A radial artery graft may be interposed
- A greater saphenous vein graft may be interposed
- Prophylactic anticoagulation therapy is not typically administered during the postoperative period

## Simultaneous Portal Vein and Hepatic Artery Resection

- This is the most technically demanding combined vascular resection procedure
- It is predominantly applied in left-sided hepatectomies
- Vascular resection followed by reconstruction is performed during the final step
- Reconstruction of the hepatic artery is performed after reconstruction of the portal vein
- The technique combines the principles of portal and arterial reconstruction

## Hepatopancreatoduodenectomy Definition

- Hepatopancreatoduodenectomy is a multivisceral resection
- It combines resection of:
  - Extrahepatic bile duct
  - Portion of the liver
  - Pancreatic head
  - Duodenum
- The main purpose is removal of the entire extrahepatic biliary system
- This includes bile duct from the ampulla of Vater up to the hilum and gallbladder

## HPD: Modes of Spread Treated

| Mode | Description |
|---|---|
| Diffuse infiltration | Tumor involves the entire extrahepatic bile duct |
| Downward spread | Perihilar tumor exhibits downward superficial spreading |
| Middle tumor invasion | Tumor infiltrates right hepatic artery and pancreatic head at advancing margin |
| Bulky nodes | Bulky nodal metastasis in pancreatoduodenal region |
| Multiple tumors | Multiple bile duct tumors |
| Positive distal stump | Unexpected cancer involvement of distal ductal stump |

## HPD: Primary Use and Controversy

- HPD is primarily applied in laterally spreading configurations
- This includes diffuse infiltration, downward superficial spreading, and unexpected distal stump involvement
- HPD remains controversial
- It is the most challenging operation
- It is the only means of treating some cholangiocarcinomas with otherwise unresectable extensive spread

## HPD: Patient Selection

- Benefits are not universal
- Benefits are limited to patients with favorable tumor biology
- Careful patient selection is critical
- Extensive disease alone is not sufficient justification
- Physiologic reserve and tumor behavior must be considered

## HPD: Operative Sequence

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| Step 1 | Pancreatoduodenectomy |
| Step 2 | Upward lymph node clearance at hepatoduodenal ligament with vascular division |
| Step 3 | Mobilization of ipsilateral hemiliver including caudate lobe |
| Step 4 | Liver parenchyma transection |
| Step 5 | Division of intrahepatic bile duct |

- The pancreatoduodenectomy-first approach is rational, useful, and easier to perform than other sequences
- In exceptional cases, a hepatectomy-first procedure might be recommended

## HPD: Reconstruction

- A modified Child's method is preferentially employed
- The pancreatic stump is anastomosed to the Roux-en-Y jejunal limb first
- The intrahepatic bile duct is anastomosed next
- The stomach or duodenum is anastomosed last
- Placement of an external stent for pancreatojejunostomy is routinely employed
- The remnant pancreas often has a soft parenchymal texture with a nondilated pancreatic duct

## Summary Table: Standard Versus Extended Resection

| Feature | Standard Resection | Extended Resection |
|---|---|---|
| Typical use | Bismuth type I to III without macrovascular invasion | Selected advanced tumors, including some Bismuth type IV |
| Liver resection | Right or left hemihepatectomy | Trisectionectomy or more extensive hepatectomy |
| Caudate lobectomy | Included | Included |
| Vascular resection | Not routine | May be required |
| Technical demand | High | Very high |

## Summary Table: Key Anatomic Pitfalls

| Structure | Pitfall |
|---|---|
| Middle hepatic artery | May originate from proper, right, or left hepatic artery |
| Right posterior hepatic artery | May run supraportal and close to hilar ducts |
| Caudate branches | Small arterial and portal branches require cautious ligation |
| Left portal vein umbilical portion | Must be fully mobilized in right trisectionectomy |
| Right hepatic vein | Must be preserved as remnant drainage in left trisectionectomy |

## Key Technical Principles

- Know the individual hilar anatomy before operation
- Perform meticulous lymphadenectomy and margin assessment
- Include caudate lobectomy routinely
- Detach the hilar plate sufficiently to obtain proximal duct margins
- Recognize arterial and portal venous anomalies early
- Preserve remnant inflow and outflow
- Use vascular reconstruction only when technically feasible and oncologically justified

## Final Take-Home Message

- Standard resection for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma is hemihepatectomy with bile duct resection, caudate lobectomy, lymphadenectomy, and bilioenteric reconstruction
- Extended resections can convert selected advanced tumors to resectable disease
- Trisectionectomy improves proximal duct margins in selected Bismuth type IV tumors
- Combined vascular resection and hepatopancreatoduodenectomy are demanding but may offer the only chance of cure in highly selected patients
- Success depends on precise anatomy, disciplined technique, and careful patient selection
